raw_response:
I'm 68 years old this year. My wife and I farm these 7.5 mu, and my son works in the county town but comes back for busy seasons. I finished middle school, so I can read fertilizer labels and understand what the extension technician tells me, but honestly, I trust what I've seen with my own eyes more than what some young person writes in a book. I've been farming this land for 20 years — I took it over from my father when I was 48 — and I know which plots hold water and which ones dry out first.

It's late April now. The winter wheat I planted last October is up to my knee and looking decent. I broadcast 80 jin of compound fertilizer per mu before planting, and now it's time to topdress at jointing. I'll put down about 30 jin of urea per mu — that's what I did last year and I got about 400 kg/mu. The extension guy says I could push to 500 kg/mu if I add more nitrogen, but fertilizer prices went up again and I need to keep some cash for the vegetable seedlings. I'd rather be a bit conservative than run out of money before the chili and eggplant are in the ground. I'll irrigate the wheat three times total: the winter irrigation is done, the green-up irrigation is done, and now I'll water once at jointing. The well is metered, so every irrigation costs me about 50 yuan for the wheat field. It adds up.

My main field — 4.5 mu — is wheat-maize double cropping. That's my bread and butter. The wheat comes off in early June, and I have maybe five days to get the maize in. I don't bother with tillage between crops — no time. I'll buy hybrid maize seed, probably Nongda 372 like last year, about 1.2 packages per mu at 60 yuan. I'll broadcast 50 jin of compound fertilizer when I plant, and that's usually enough. If the plants look yellow in July, I might topdress a little urea, but last year I didn't and still got 440 kg/mu. Maize needs two irrigations in a normal summer, three if it's dry. I'll see how the rain goes.

The other 3 mu near the house is my vegetable plot. I put 1.5 mu in cabbage this spring — I transplanted the seedlings in mid-March. Cabbage needs a lot of fertilizer, so I put down chicken manure plus compound at planting, and I'll topdress with urea once in May. It needs water more often than grain, so I'll irrigate four times. I should get about 3,000 kg per mu by mid-June if the worms don't get it.

For the chili and eggplant, I'm buying seedlings from the market in early May — 0.8 mu of chili and 0.7 mu of eggplant. I don't have a greenhouse to start my own, and at my age it's easier to just buy them. They're expensive though: about 200 yuan per mu for chili seedlings and 180 for eggplant. Both need plenty of water and pesticide. Chili especially gets aphids and virus, so I'll spray insecticide and fungicide three or four times. Eggplant needs similar care. The vegetable plot is where I actually make money per mu, but it's also where I spend money. If the market price for chili drops, I could lose out.

Here's my problem: cash flow. I need to buy maize seed, pay for the vegetable seedlings, and buy more fertilizer for the cabbage topdressing all in the next month. That's about 2,500 yuan right there. I have some savings from last year's maize, but my grandson's school fees are coming up. So I'm cutting back where I can: I'm using saved wheat seed this year instead of buying new certified seed, I'll do more hand-weeding on the vegetables instead of buying expensive herbicide, and if the summer rain is decent, I might skip one irrigation on the maize. My neighbor Li spent a fortune on precision fertilizer for his wheat, but I'm 68. My yields are stable, my family is fed, and I sleep fine at night. Good enough is good enough.
